strengths: The manuscript tackles an important challenge in machine learning by focusing on out-of-distribution (OOD) data handling for tabular datasets.
The paper introduces Tabular Contrast Learning (TCL) as a novel solution.
The problem is well-defined with significant practical implications, especially for general users with computational limitations.
The authors have provided a clear motivation for their work, particularly in making OOD detection and handling accessible without high-end hardware requirements.
The proposed TCL method appears promising for addressing efficiency and accuracy in tabular OOD tasks.
The research addresses an important issue in machine learning—handling OOD data, which is crucial for ensuring model reliability and robustness.
TCL demonstrates a very efficient approach that reduces computational costs, making it viable for deployment in environments with limited resources.
The proposed method is easy to understand, with a clear problem statement and definition.
Simaltaneously considering the OOD problem with efficiency may be an interesting direction, especially in the realm of large-scale models.
weaknesses: Many of the main claims in the abstract lack support or are difficult to verify -- for example, "Addressing OOD data requires extensive fine-tuning and experimental trials" and "Deep learning has been suggested as a solution and has shown significant improvements".
The paper is missing references to many relevant works, including: Malinin et al. (2022); Gardner et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2024) (all propose benchmarks for OOD-related tabular tasks).

The paper is also missing references to several relevant empirical studies for tabular data, including: Gardner et al. (2022); Grinsztajn et al. (2022); Kadra et al. (2021) (these suggest GBDTs are appropriate baselines, which are omitted).

Contrastive learning has already been widely used for tabular data; see e.g. Bahri et al. (2021) and Rabbani et al. (2024); its performance has generally not been competitive with strong baselines and adoption has been limited.
The paper simply applies an existing method (Contrastive Federated Learning, or CFL) to tabular data, which is not sufficient for acceptance given concerns with the empirical evaluations.

More detail should be provided on the datasets in the main text, including justification for using generic tabular datasets (e.g., Adult, California Housing) for OOD detection and descriptive statistics.
The paper is quite difficult to read in places due to grammatical issues; proofreading by a native English speaker is suggested.
Definition 4: "eucledian".

It would benefit from a more detailed comparison with recent advancements in tabular contrastive learning; two works could provide relevant baselines: "Best of Both Worlds: Multimodal Contrastive Learning With Tabular and Imaging Data" (CVPR23) and "TabContrast: A Local-Global Level Method for Tabular Contrastive Learning" (NIPS23).
Why is the Contrastive Federated Learning (CFL) reference in an anonymized link?
Why does the title miss some keywords like Tabular Contrastive Learning?
Why is there no experiment for baseline models running on CPU (Apple) to fairly compare with your TCL?
The experimental results are not particularly impressive; while TCL shows high efficiency, it only achieved optimal performance on three datasets compared to FT‑T and ResNet.

The paper lacks a comprehensive comparison of methods; it should include comparisons with GBDT methods (e.g., CatBoost[1], XGBoost[2]), other state-of-the-art deep learning models (e.g., TabR[3], ExcelFormer[4], Trompt[5]), and alternative self‑supervised learning algorithms (e.g., Scarf[6], VIME[7]) besides SubTab.

More details should be included in the paper, such as the specific structure of TCL, the downstream classifier used, hyperparameters of the comparison methods, and whether experiments were conducted multiple times to present average results.

The experiment comparing dot product and Euclidean distance indicates that dot product is more efficient on the hardware they used, but the work does not discuss how using these two distance metrics impacts TCL performance and the significance of computational time for distance calculation within the entire TCL process.
The paper presentation should be improved; the abstract issues in existing OOD works do not appear novel, and extensive fine‑tuning and experimental trials are not unique to this OOD problem.

The review of related works requires significant improvement; the authors discuss only two methods in Sec. 2.1 and one other in L38, with the most recent paper referenced from 2017, and should put more effort into the literature review (e.g., [1]).

The proposed TCL employs a common strategy—contrastive learning with two views and a classification/regression head—that has been used in various contrastive learning‑based tabular models such as SubTab; its performance is not superior to the selected baselines, limiting novelty and effectiveness.
The selected baselines are based on the work of Gorishniy et al., 2021; many advanced tabular prediction models have emerged since and should be included (e.g., summarized in [2]).

The authors used CPUs to train their model but used an H100 GPU for the baselines, which is confusing; there is no specific design element that makes the proposed method more efficient, and matrix augmentation appears to require more computational resources; Table 4's training durations lack clarity regarding parameter space equality across models.
